records.issue_text: [BUG] The client rejects previously-failed emails with the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') message even when the server rejected the email with the specific 'user.email.blocked' reason, because the server error text is discarded in favor of a hardcoded client-side message. A user whose email was blocked by a moderator sees 'user.email.invalid' (implying a malformed address) instead of the distinct 'is not allowed' message the diff added, sending them on a futile hunt for a typo rather than telling them the address is disallowed.

records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail#should_block? performs a read-modify-write on match_count (record.match_count += 1; record.save) with no atomic UPDATE, so concurrent requests both read the same count and one increment is lost. Two simultaneous signup attempts with the same blocked email both load count=N and both save N+1; match_count and last_match_at drift permanently downward relative to real match volume, and under Rails' stale-object save the whole row write can also clobber concurrent updates. Use update_all("match_count = match_count + 1") instead.
records.rationale: In `app/models/blocked_email.rb`, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does a non-atomic read/modify/write: it loads a row (`record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`), then mutates fields in memory (`record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now`) and persists with `record.save`. With concurrent calls for the same email, both can read the same `match_count` and overwrite each other’s increments/`last_match_at`, causing lost updates. The diff contains no locking (`lock!`) or atomic SQL increment (`update_all`/`increment_counter`), so the race described is verifiable from this ch

Use update_all("match_count = match_count + 1") instead.

records.issue_text: [BUG] The domain restriction logic (email_domains_whitelist/blacklist) was moved into EmailValidator but the blocked-email check is gated behind `record.errors[attribute].blank?`, meaning when a whitelist/blacklist error is added the should_block? side-effect is skipped, so the same email yields different match statistics depending on which restriction fires. Operators loading blocked_emails rows to audit 'has this email ever been blocked' (the exact use case the last_match_at spec comment describes) get silently missing match records for any email that also trips the domain restriction, because validation bails before the BlockedEmail lookup/write.
records.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the blocked-email check (which calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` and updates `match_count`/`last_match_at`) is explicitly gated by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. Since the whitelist/blacklist logic above can add `record.errors.add(attribute, ...)`, any email that trips those domain restrictions will skip `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so its match statistics will not be recorded. This matches the finding’s claim about missing audit stats when domain restrictions fire.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs writes (incrementing match_count and updating last_match_at) inside model validation, so the statistics no longer measure blocks — they measure every validation attempt of a previously-blocked address. Any failed signup attempt that re-validates the same blocked email (wrong password, taken username, retry) inflates match_count, and last_match_at becomes 'last attempted' rather than 'last blocked', defeating the stated purpose of the last_match_at spec comment ("we can see whether those emails have ever been blocked").

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The BlockedEmail check is skipped whenever any earlier error was added to :email (e.g. a uniqueness failure), so a blocked email that is also taken never gets recorded as blocked and never produces the blocked error. A user whose blocked email is also already registered sees only 'has already been taken' in full_messages, and because the client-side rejectedEmails gating depends on result.errors.email being present while the reason shown is the generic invalid string, the block semantics differ by which unrelated validation fires first.

records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write (record.save) inside model validation, so every validation attempt — including saves that fail for other reasons and repeated resubmissions of the same signup form — increments match_count and updates last_match_at. records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.where(email: email) matches case-sensitively while User emails are normalized to lowercase, so a blocked_emails row loaded with mixed-case (e.g. 'Spammer@Example.com', the only way to populate the table since this diff adds no writer) never blocks the corresponding user address. Operators who seed the table directly (there is no admin UI/rake path in this diff) get silent non-blocking for any row whose case doesn't exactly match the downcased user input.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The email domain whitelist/blacklist check now runs only when email_changed?, but EmailValidator is also a shared generic validator available to any model; combined with the removal of the model-local email_in_restriction_setting?, any existing code paths that relied on email domain restrictions being enforced on create with an unchanged/assigned email (e.g. mass-created or seeded users) skip the check entirely. Signup flows that set email via mass assignment then save (email_changed? true on create, so mostly safe) — but any later rework that reloads/assigns email outside change-tracking bypasses both the domain restriction and the BlockedEmail check, letting blacklisted-domain accounts through.
records.rationale: The finding claims the domain whitelist/blacklist check “now runs only when email_changed?”, causing new skipping behavior. But in the diff, the old implementation already only ran on `email_changed?`: `-  validate :email_validator, if: :email_changed?` and the new one keeps the same condition: `+  validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`. So no new bypass is introduced by this change; the rest of the finding is speculative about other models/code paths not shown in the diff.
